title: Fish removed. Recovery still lagged.
paper_title: Pharmaceutical Pollution Alters the Structure of Freshwater Communities and Hinders Their Recovery from a Fish Predator
citation: Michelangeli et al. (2024), Environ. Sci. Technol.
summary: In 12 outdoor mesocosms, zooplankton abundance rebounded less in fluoxetine-exposed treatments than in controls after fish removal. Fluoxetine dosing continued during this recovery period.
evidence_note: Four tanks per treatment; responses varied and estimates were uncertain. The experiment did not establish the mechanism, test recovery after drug removal, or measure diversity loss. Nutrient addition confounded attribution of the initial zooplankton decline solely to fish.
review_note: Full-text design, timeline, results and caveats checked on 2026-11-07; see evidence/tt-003.md. Quota and current live-media inspection remain required before scheduling.

posts.caption:
TT-003-REEL | FISH REMOVED. RECOVERY STILL LAGGED.

Does removing one pressure guarantee recovery when another remains?

Researchers created 12 outdoor freshwater tank communities, with four tanks per treatment. All received mosquitofish; some later received fluoxetine, an antidepressant, while others were solvent controls.

After fish removal, zooplankton abundance rebounded less in the fluoxetine treatments than in controls. Important: drug dosing continued for the 21-day post-removal period. This was not evidence of permanent damage after pollution stopped.

Responses varied between tanks and estimates were uncertain. The mechanism was not established. Nutrients were also added before fish introduction, so the initial zooplankton decline cannot be attributed solely to fish. These were simplified outdoor communities, not whole lakes.

Original research: Michelangeli et al. (2024), Environmental Science & Technology.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c02807
Research library: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/#tt-003-recovery-with-pollution
